 Michael Burry warns AI stocks mirror 1929 and 2000 crashes — and singles out Nvidia's risky deals
 Eric Esposito Fri, November 20, 2026 at 4:30 PM CST 5 min read NVDA -10.94% 
 Is Michael Burry's doomsday vision coming to fruition? 
 Given the ugly price action in AI stocks, it's getting harder to argue with "The Big Short" star's bearish thesis.

 In a recent X post , the famed investor reminded readers: "I tried to warn you all." He's referring to AI-related companies he publicly shorted over the past few years. In addition to the entire semiconductor industry, Burry called out GPU giant Nvidia and neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius. 
 Although Burry claimed he "didn't say short" any of these companies, he maintains that he "provided the information one would need to sell." 
 And Burry doesn't seem to see a bottom for the tech market anytime soon. In another X post , he compared today's market volatility to historic crashes in 1929 and 2000. Burry's primary reason for this correlation is "the lack of a proximate cause in earnings." 
 On Substack , Burry expanded on this point, admitting that, although today's market leaders are "killing it with respect to earnings," that's no reason to expect higher prices. He cited articles from 1929 and 2000 to show how investors were in "complete shock that stocks were falling despite good news in earnings." The same phenomenon, Burry argued, is at play today with AI companies.​ 
 To bolster his bearish thesis, Burry highlighted two other points. First, the peaks of the 1929 and 2000 rallies "predated real business deterioration by a year or so." Second, plenty of "bear market rallies" can follow a major collapse. According to his analysis, these false signs of hope had averaged 22% in bearish periods between 1929 - 1932 and 2000 - 2002.​ 
 Burry sees danger behind Nvidia's dazzling numbers 
 ​On X, Futurum Equities' Chief Market Strategist Shay Boloor pushed back against Burry's warnings, claiming Burry couldn't have predicted multiple black swan events that precipitated today's drawdown. Specifically, Boloor pointed to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's shocking resignation and Democrats winning traditionally red states like Texas. 
 ​In response, Burry said, "If you think this is still all about an affair and some politics, you're not thinking hard enough."​ 
 Story Continues As the Jensen Huang scandal continues to unravel, Burry has been putting out more articles critical of Nvidia's business deals and their impact on the AI space. 
 For instance, on November 13, Burry wrote on X that his "thesis on NVIDIA was not about illicit affairs because it goes far beyond illicit affairs." He then quoted a Wall Street Journal article alleging Jensen Huang was taking excessive financial risks to keep up demand for Nvidia chips.​ 
 Burry argued these questionable circular financing deals were "why the stock wasn't performing and kept getting 'cheaper,' even before the affairs came to light." 
 Another question Burry has with Nvidia is just how many of its chips made their way to the Asian market without government approval. In another X post , he commented on data suggesting some of the largest AI labs in China have been using banned Nvidia chips. 
 As Burry said: "This is no surprise to analysts who years ago questioned SE Asia/Singapore's need for so many advanced $NVDA chips. The real reveal would be evidence that NVDA booked more revenue and profit from Asia than it had let on."

 Should everyone bail on the stock market?​ 
 Whether investors believe Burry's predictions or not, there's no denying today's drawdowns are scary. For instance, at the time of writing, Nvidia 's year-to-date performance is down about 27%, while riskier neoclouds like CoreWeave are in the red by roughly 43%. All of this selling pressure pushed the tech-heavy NASDAQ into slightly negative territory for 2026. 
 At the time of writing, even diversified funds like the S&P 500 are now only up about 2% year-to-date. 
 It can feel tempting during these times to join the crowd and panic-dump your portfolio. While everyone's situation is different, keep in mind that steep corrections in major indices are far from unusual. 
 Data from Teachers Insurance and Annuity Association of America (TIAA) puts drawdowns into perspective. Declines of at least 5% in the S&P 500 happened in 94% of years post-1928. Even steeper dips of 10% or more happened in 63% of years throughout this period. 
 Thankfully, rebounds are also common. For example, TIAA noted that although the S&P dropped 25% intra-year in 2022, it came roaring back in the subsequent three years with gains of 24%, 23%, and 16%, respectively. 
 Of course, there are no guarantees on future prices, and people exposed to individual companies may have to make tougher decisions. However, history suggests that large diversified funds like the S&P 500 eventually shrug off even the worst of selloffs.
